results.summary:
The Lazarus Group has launched Operation FlashHole, a sophisticated espionage campaign targeting South Korean organizations by exploiting mandatory financial security software to deliver advanced, modular malware chains.

### Key Points
- The campaign targets South Korean firms in the software, construction, and wired communication equipment sectors using spear-phishing and watering-hole strategies.
- Attackers abuse the legitimate INISAFE CrossWeb EX software to execute malicious payloads, including TechHub, Cubridge, and the newly identified ClientHub.
- The group utilizes AI-generated content for lure websites and incorporates post-quantum cryptography to conceal its sophisticated, in-memory malware delivery framework.
- Evidence suggests the operation began in July 2025, shortly after the conclusion of the group's previous Operation SyncHole campaign.
- The modular toolkit includes specialized plugins for data exfiltration, process monitoring, and credential theft, demonstrating a highly segmented and evolving operational structure.

### Why it Matters
This campaign highlights the significant security risks posed by mandatory software that creates a persistent, high-integrity attack surface for sophisticated threat actors. As the Lazarus Group continues to refine its espionage techniques and adopt advanced encryption, organizations must prioritize the transition away from vulnerable legacy security software to mitigate these evolving threats.

results.title: Can James Carville Please Just Be Quietly Wrong Somewhere Else?
results.author: Elizabeth Spiers
results.content:
Can James Carville Please Just Be Quietly Wrong Somewhere Else?
The omnipresent consultant-cum-tantrum-thrower has long outlived whatever relevance he once had, but cable producers, podcast hosts, and Democratic campaigns haven’t got the memo.
Right now there are hundreds of Democratic fundraising e-mails in my inbox, putatively from former Democratic strategist James Carville. If I wanted to avoid them entirely, I could block or unsubscribe from the various campaigns and PACs sponsoring them, but that would not prevent me from having to listen to Carville give terrible advice to Democrats. That’s because he’s also a regular on cable news, heavily quoted in newspaper and magazine articles about election prospects for the party, and an interview subject on seemingly all of America’s political podcasts.
He recently appeared with Bill Kristol on a podcast hosted by The Bulwark and stated that he’d rather Republicans keep the House by a five-member majority after the midterms than have Democrats win, because then “they’re hostage to the DSA.” The Daily Beast, long tethered to a clickbait-through-faux-outrage business model, ran an account of Carville’s comments under the sensationalistic headline “Top Dem Strategist Makes Shock Midterms Wish.” Unfortunately, though, the fact that Carville is bashing progressives and suggesting they’re worse than Republicans is not shocking at all: He’s been doing that for years now, at every opportunity.
This has put me in the uncomfortable position of trusting Carville less than Bill Kristol, one of the architects of the Iraq War and a Republican conservative turned Never Trumper. Unlike Carville, Kristol at least seems to understand what progressives stand for and occasionally concedes that they have good points. “I don’t agree with people saying ICE and CBP need ‘more training,’” Kristol wrote on Bluesky recently. “They’re doing exactly what this administration has trained them to—impose a reign of fear in blue cities. They don’t need more training. They need to be ripped up root and branch.” In the absurdist political world of 2026, in other words, we have Bill Kristol calling for ICE to be abolished, and James Carville rooting for ongoing Republican rule in Congress in lieu of having his political sensibilities unpleasantly challenged.
Carville loathes the left in a knee-jerk way that isn’t backed by any serious thoughtfulness about what progressives want—or even what voters at large want. A majority of Democrats want Medicare for All. Seventy-four percent of Democrats want to tax the rich more. Four in 10 Americans (not just Democrats!) think capitalism isn’t helping them and are open to socialist solutions to some problems. Sixty-four percent of Americans think we should give Israel less military and financial support. These are all things that Carville and his cohort of 1990s-era political power brokers like to characterize as views held by tiny, unrealistic, and leftist minorities.
Carville often distorts the positions of the Democratic Socialists in particular, intentionally reinforcing negative characterizations lofted by fellow pundits at one of his preferred outlets for bloviating, Fox News. In August he criticized a DSA candidate on the basis that he “has the attribute of every DSA member in the country, and that is he has a motor mouth.”
James Carville complaining that someone who is not James Carville has a motor mouth is like Donald Trump complaining that someone who is not Donald Trump has a reputation for bankrupting casinos. But self-awareness is not Carville’s strong suit generally. He also likes to mouth loyalty to the working classes, playing up his “ragin’ Cajun’” persona while being married to a former Republican consultant and from the comfort of one of his multiple multimillion-dollar homes.
Still, Carville’s greatest offense is continuing to live in the reality of Clinton-era politics while spouting advice to those of us who live here in 2026. Some of this might be chalked up to age and complacency. Carville wouldn’t be the first 81-year-old who doesn’t have his finger on the pulse of what anyone under the age of 40 is thinking or doing. He’s also not the first man to enjoy early success and dine out on it for decades—or to assume that the expertise founded on that achievement is stable over time and does not need to be refreshed or reassessed as circumstances change. He is also not the only Democrat to trot out a ’90s-era political playbook posited on the vital role played by s a nebulous center of reasonable moderates in the electorate who switch back and forth between parties. Nor is he the only aging centrist who believes, wrongly, that the far left is as dangerous as the far right.
But he is one of the people who can’t stop talking about it. And for some inexplicable reason, he’s the outraged centrist whom the media can’t stop platforming as an avatar for mainstream Democratic politics—even as he stubbornly refuses to educate himself about who progressives are and what they want, beyond crude ideological caricatures that wouldn’t be out of place in the editorial pages of The Wall Street Journal.
He’s also still leaning on the idea that elections are about one issue: the economy. I watched D.A. Pennebaker’s The War Room three years after it came out, in a political science class taught by a former Republican consultant. I don’t remember any specific lines from it except Carville’s “it’s the economy, stupid” mantra, which, more than anything, defined Carville’s brand as a strategist to the public. Like many early Carville-isms, there was truth to it, but it was also an oversimplification. Voters are always driven by economic concerns, but elections are never about one thing—even Bill Clinton’s victory over George H.W. Bush, in the midst of a deep recession, was driven by increasing disillusionment with the first Iraq War, Clinton’s personal charisma and media savviness, and a host of other things that had little to do with the real economy.
We’re in much the same position now, as voters are angry over the state of the economy, but also register strong sentiments against rampant corruption and threats to democracy. Nevertheless, Carville is relentlessly on his 1992 message, trotting out a variation of “it’s the economy, stupid” on the countless occasions he’s in front of a camera or podcast mic. In a recent Fox News appearance, he brayed that Democrats need to avoid culture-war issues and identity politics and just focus on the economy. “quit f—ing around with all this cultural stuff and start talking about people’s wages…. Start talking about what we can do to protect people who are trying to make it and particularly young people.”
By protecting young people who are trying to make it, he did not mean protecting immigrants as they seek to avoid violence and detention from ICE, young women who need abortions, or young Black men who don’t want to be killed or beaten by the police. Nor was he referring to young trans people who end up murdered because the right paints them as sexual deviants or pedophiles, and people in Carville’s cohort nod solemnly and say maybe they have a point about trans women in sports. He’s talking about wages and the ability of young people to find jobs.
All politics are identity politics on some level, but like many white straight men of a certain age, Carville doesn’t consider “white straight male” an identity. It’s simply the cultural default in his view of America. He assumes the priorities of the liberal or liberal-leaning white straight man are generally good for everybody else.
But in reality, you cannot separate culture from politics, or identity from politics. Politics is about power and its uses—and elections are about who should have it. Voter perception of the economy is heavily driven by vibes in part because the metrics of the real economy—GDP, productivity growth, even inflation—don’t necessarily reflect the situation on the ground for people. Feelings of financial security are often proxies for whether people feel safe and satisfied generally.
In other words, what constitutes a kitchen-table issue—to use the refrain favored by Carville and the centrist Democratic consultant class—depends on whose kitchen table you’re sitting at. If you’re a young woman being forced to carry a baby you don’t want and bankrupted by medical bills for complications or an unexpected C-section, your earnings potential limited because now you’re not going to college and there’s a lower ceiling on your earning potential, that’s an economic issue as well as a bodily autonomy issue.
And you cannot talk persuasively about affordability without talking about class mobility via education. That ideal is under sustained attack from Republicans who oppose DEI on the basis that they do not want women and minorities in power. Meanwhile, our political economy teems with other practical obstacles afflicting the life chances of members of less-resourced communities, from the administrative burdens of receiving public assistance (some of which, it must be said, were created by Bill Clinton’s welfare “reforms”) to the increasing cost of caring for an aging population. The country’s manifold healthcare crisis—a key driver of affordability—has been made far worse by things like caretakers’ being detained and deported and ob-gyns’ withholding care because they fear criminal prosecution for treating complications in pregnancies. It’s affordability, stupid—but not to the exclusion of the things that Carville dismisses as culture war issues. In many cases, it’s an affordability issue because of these things.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Much of Carville’s analysis is facile and blinkered because he does not understand that the electoral environment of 2026 is not the electoral environment of 1992. “It’s negative partisanship, stupid” may not be the pithiest slogan, but it applies much more directly to politics in the Trump era than Carville’s nostrums do. There is no persuading the GOP to make common cause with Democrats—which is why Republican candidates never attempt it or talk about it. But like many self-identified centrist Boomers, Carville spends more energy reaching across the aisle to hypothetical swing voters than he does attending to the real-world plight of core Democratic constituencies.
Progressives—including the DSA members and candidates Carville keeps insulting—overwhelmingly supported Kamala Harris in the last election, far more so than the weaker independent coalitions Carville seems to want to reach with his Fox News appearances. Progressives exhibit the highest levels of political engagement in the Democratic coalition, yet Carville keeps insisting that Democrats win elections in spite of them rather than because of them.
I won’t pretend to know whether he does this because he’s genuinely ignorant of these facts, or because he just sympathizes more with neoliberal interests and thinks that if he paints the left as fringe-y, impractical, or stupid, that voters will internalize that message and pull the core Democratic electorate rightward. If Carville keeps suggesting that any Democrat’s association with Hasan Piker—a streamer he’d never heard of before this election cycle—is a bigger problem for Democrats than the associations of congressional Republicans with assorted white supremacists, technofascist interests, and Donald Trump himself, I’ll assume that Carville actually wants a Democratic Party made up of MAGA collaborationists. Either way, he does Democrats no favors, because that’s not what voters have told us—repeatedly—they want.
When I ponder the stubborn tenacity of Carville’s pundit career, I keep thinking about a recent Wired article titled “Men Can’t Stop Faking How Much They Know About AI.” That headline is not exactly surprising to me, since I’ve had men explain AI incorrectly to me as recently as yesterday. (I’m a former tech equity analyst and cohost a financial news podcast, but I am also a girl, you understand.) But the phony claims to expertise from American men catalogued in the Wired story have strong correlations with Carville-style punditry: One Harvard study cited in the piece found that when quizzed about AI leaders, men were more likely to confidently assert that they knew who specific people were—even when the names presented to them were fictional. They were also less likely to admit that they didn’t know the answer to a question.
Carville fits the same dreary profile: He’s overconfident about what thinks he knows and will not admit to what he doesn’t. Democrats and media organizations do not need to keep giving him a megaphone. There are plenty of smart people in Democratic political circles who have worked on an actual campaign since the turn of the century, who have informed and helpful things to say, and who understand that the Trump-era GOP is not analogous to prior GOP regimes. Nor do they uncritically assume that today’s Democratic constituencies are analogous to the coalition that put Bill Clinton in office.
James Carville has plenty of money, social connections, and leisure pursuits to keep him busy—which is more than most Americans get to enjoy during their retirement years. If he really wants to help Democrats, he might put his energies there—or at the very least, step back, stop talking, and see if he might, at long last, learn how to listen.

results.title: Apple is looking for a cellular modem engineer to help shape its transition to 6G
results.author: Marcus Mendes
results.content:
Apple is looking for an experienced cellular modem systems engineer to help develop its next generation of cellular modems as the company transitions toward 6G. Here are the details.
‘A rare opportunity to shape the future of wireless communication’
As spotted by MacRumors, Apple listed a new job opening yesterday for a 6G Cellular Modem Systems Engineer, with a base salary range of $175,000 to $308,500 per year, plus stock awards and other benefits.
From the job listing:
We’re looking for a Cellular Modem Systems Engineer to join our cellular systems engineering team as we define and build the next generation of cellular technology. This is a rare opportunity to shape the future of wireless communication at a company that ships at global scale as we transition towards 6G. In this role, you’ll bring an end-to-end view of wireless systems — spanning 3GPP standards, feature definition and planning, design, hardware and software architecture and partitioning — to deliver leading-edge performance and power optimizations and features that directly improve the user experience across Apple products. If you thrive at the intersection of deep technical theory and hands-on bring-up — and you’re excited about pushing beyond 5G into the 6G era — we want to hear from you.
Apple says the candidate’s responsibilities will include defining features and requirements for next-generation cellular modems, designing algorithms to improve performance and power efficiency, and working with hardware and software teams to bring those technologies to market.
The candidate should have a degree in electrical engineering, computer engineering, or a related field, along with at least 10 years of industry experience working with cellular technologies.
Apple also requires a strong understanding of cellular communication standards and proficiency in MATLAB, C/C++, or Python.
Interestingly, Apple also lists experience with generative AI and LLM-based tools “to accelerate engineering workflows” as a minimum qualification. Ideally, the candidate should also have a track record of published research or patents in wireless communications, among other preferred qualifications.
For context, 6G is still years away and in the early stages of development, as companies and industry organizations work to define what it will look like.
Top comment by Tudor
I really wonder why we never push existing technology to its limits before moving on to something that’s much crazier and that we will never achieve either.
I don’t recall 5G in practice being anywhere near 20Gbps. Not even 5Gbps. Heck, in most cases, it’s not even 2Gbps. And now we’re done with it and moving to 6G already?
The International Telecommunication Union (ITU) has outlined potential peak speeds of up to 200 Gbps, compared to 5G’s theoretical maximum of 20 Gbps, along with research targets for latency as low as 0.1 milliseconds.
AI is also expected to play a much bigger role in 6G, helping networks automatically adjust to changing conditions, optimize signal quality, manage traffic, and reduce power consumption.
The first official 6G technical specifications are expected to be finalized in late 2028, with commercial networks and compatible devices anticipated around 2030.

results.title: This copy-paste scam surged 517% in six months, enable this setting to let Chrome catch it
results.author: Hamed Paydarfar
results.content:
In recent years, ClickFix has become one of the fastest-growing scams that tricks people into copying and running malicious commands on their computers. Google is now giving Chrome a new layer of defense against it. According to the company's official announcement, the browser can now analyze suspicious commands copied from webpages and warn users before they unintentionally install malware.
Earlier, ESET recorded a 517% surge in ClickFix detections over six months. By H1 2025, it had become the second most common attack vector, right behind phishing scams. However, Chrome’s new defense is not enabled for everyone by default.
Chrome helps you catch commands hidden behind fake error messages
But you need Enhanced Protection turned on to receive warnings
ClickFix attacks partly rely on steps carried out by unsuspecting users. They usually involve a malicious webpage that displays a fake error, browser-update prompt, virus warning, or CAPTCHA alongside instructions for supposedly fixing the problem yourself.
We've previously covered the kind of fake CAPTCHA you should never complete. These fake CAPTCHAs usually instruct you to open Windows Run or Terminal and paste a command that, sometimes, doesn't even match the text displayed on the webpage. Running such commands can install malware on Windows, macOS, or Linux, so don't assume that macOS or a highly secure Linux-based OS is immune to this.
ClickFix malware attacks have become extremely common nowadays, but Google is targeting the moment between the scammer placing a command on your computer's clipboard and you pasting it somewhere within the OS. The solution comes as an additional feature under Chrome's Enhanced Protection option, which already helps determine whether a site is real or a scam.
Google's expanded defenses allow Chrome to scrub personal information from the clipboard payload and send it to Safe Browsing for analysis. If the command is deemed dangerous, Chrome displays a warning. Separately, Gemini examines a page's claimed brand and intent, and Chrome combines that analysis with its domain reputation and other security signals to reach a verdict. To enable these protections, open Chrome’s Settings, select Privacy and security, open Security, and choose Enhanced protection.
While Chrome's latest defense helps users avoid one of the most dangerous online scams, knowing how to recognize a fake virus alert remains worthwhile because no browser protection can eliminate social engineering entirely. Generally speaking, no legitimate webpage should require you to paste and run mysterious commands on your computer.

results.title: How To Change IP Address On iPhone: 7 Free Ways
results.author: M Asad
results.content:
You can change your iPhone’s IP address for free in a few taps. The right method depends on which of your iPhone’s two IP addresses you want to change.
One is the local IP your Wi-Fi router gives your iPhone. The other is the public IP that every website and app sees, and it’s the one most people want to change.
The quickest way to get a new public IP is a free VPN tool. It sends your traffic through a server in a location you pick, so websites see that server’s IP address instead of yours. It also encrypts your connection, which matters on hotel and café Wi-Fi.
TL;DR
Six methods change your public IP, and one changes your local IP:
| Method | IP Changed | Encrypts Traffic | Speed | Best For | 
| VPN | Public | Yes | Slight drop | Privacy, choosing a location | 
| Onion Browser (Tor) | Public, in the app only | Yes, in the app | Slow | Anonymous browsing | 
| Proxy server | Public, one tab or one Wi-Fi network | Mostly no | Varies | A quick change for one site | 
| Router restart | Public, home Wi-Fi | No | Unchanged | Refreshing a dynamic IP | 
| Different network | Public | No | Varies | The quickest change | 
| ISP request | Public | No | Unchanged | Static IP changes | 
| Manual setup | Local | No | Unchanged | Fixing local IP conflicts | 
What Is an IP Address?
An IP address is your device’s address on a network. Data uses it to find you, the way a delivery driver uses a street address. Your internet service provider (ISP) or wireless carrier gives you a public IP, and your router gives each device at home a local one.
Types of IP Addresses
Your iPhone uses both:
- Public IP address: Your ISP assigns it to your home router, or your carrier assigns it to your iPhone on cellular data. Every device on your Wi-Fi shares it, and it’s the IP websites see.
- Local IP address: Your router gives each device on your network its own address, also known as a private IP. It only works inside your network.
Think of the public IP as an apartment building’s street address and the local IP as your apartment number. Outsiders only see the street address, so that’s the one most people need to change.
One setting confuses people: Private Wi-Fi Address changes your iPhone’s MAC address, a hardware ID, not its IP address.
Why Change Your IP Address on iPhone?
For a Private IP Address
Changing your local IP fixes home network problems, not privacy ones:
- IP conflicts: Two devices get the same local address, and one drops off the network.
- Network testing: A fixed address makes it easier to test connections between devices.
- Device rules: Your router can apply settings to an address reserved for your iPhone.
For a Public IP Address
This changes what websites see:
- Privacy: Ad networks and websites use your IP to connect your visits and guess your location. A new IP cuts that link.
- Public Wi-Fi: On hotel, airport or café Wi-Fi, a VPN gives you a new IP and encrypts your traffic.
- Travel: Abroad, a server in your home country lets your accounts see a familiar location.
Note your current IP before you start so you can confirm the change.
How to Find Your IP Address on iPhone
Find Your Local IP Address
Step 1: Open Settings and tap Wi-Fi.
Step 2: Tap the More Info button (the “i” icon) next to your network.
Step 3: Look for IP Address under IPv4 Address. That’s your local IP.
Find Your Public IP Address
Settings doesn’t show your public IP. Open Safari and visit an IP lookup site, which shows your public IP, your ISP and your approximate location.
How to Change Your Public IP Address on iPhone
Ways 1 to 6 change your public IP. The seventh method, for your local IP, has its own section below.
Way 1: Use a VPN
Best for: Privacy and choosing a location.
A VPN is the simplest way to change your public IP on iPhone. You choose the server location, and the connection between your iPhone and the server is encrypted.
If you don’t want to pay, X-VPN’s free iPhone app covers the basics. There’s no account to create and no data cap, and you can pick from 26 free locations in 15 countries. Your traffic is encrypted with AES-256-GCM.
Step 1: Download X-VPN from the App Store and open it. You don’t need to sign up.
Step 2: Tap Server Select.
Step 3: Choose a free location and connect. Your public IP is now the server’s.
Pros: Quick setup, your choice of location, and encrypted traffic on any network.
Cons: Encryption costs a little speed, and the free app shows ads and has fewer locations than the paid plan.
Way 2: Use Onion Browser (Tor)
Best for: Anonymous browsing.
Tor sends your traffic through three volunteer-run relays, so websites see the last relay’s IP. There’s no official Tor Browser for iPhone. The Tor Project recommends Onion Browser, a free, open-source app.
Step 1: Download Onion Browser from the App Store.
Step 2: Open it and connect to Tor.
Step 3: Browse inside the app. The sites you visit see a Tor IP address.
Pros: Free, with strong anonymity.
Cons: It’s slow, you can’t easily pick a country, some sites refuse Tor traffic, and only pages in the app get the new IP. Apple also makes iOS browsers use WebKit, which limits Onion Browser’s privacy protections.
Way 3: Use a Proxy Server
Best for: A quick change for one site.
A proxy sits between you and a website, so the site sees the proxy’s IP. Most free proxies don’t encrypt anything, which leaves your data readable.
Option 1: In Settings. Go to Settings > Wi-Fi, tap the More Info button next to your network, then tap Configure Proxy > Manual. Enter the server and port from your proxy provider and tap Save. It only applies to that network.
Option 2: With a web proxy. Open a web proxy site in Safari and enter the site you want to visit. Only that tab uses the proxy’s IP.
Pros: Free and fast for a one-off site visit.
Cons: Most free proxies don’t encrypt, the operator can see your traffic, and the new IP stays in one tab or on one network.
Way 4: Restart Your Router
Best for: Refreshing a dynamic IP at home.
If your ISP gives you a dynamic IP, a router restart can get you a new one. It only works on Wi-Fi.
Step 1: Unplug your router.
Step 2: Wait 10 to 15 minutes. The longer you wait, the better your chances of a new address.
Step 3: Plug it back in, rejoin Wi-Fi and check your public IP.
Pros: Free, no apps, and ideal for home Wi-Fi.
Cons: It only works with dynamic IPs, your ISP may give you the same address, and it does nothing for cellular data. The new IP also stays in the same area, so use a VPN if you want a different location.
Way 5: Use a Different Network
Best for: The quickest change.
Every network has its own public IP, so switching networks gets you a new one right away.
Step 1: Disconnect from your current network.
Step 2: Connect to a different one: cellular data, another Wi-Fi network or a friend’s hotspot.
On cellular data, turning Airplane Mode on and off in Settings often gets you a new IP from your carrier.
Pros: Instant, free and no tools needed.

Step 3: Enter the IP address, Subnet Mask and Router, then tap Save.
Step 4: Reconnect to the Wi-Fi network to apply the new local IP.
Use an address in your router’s range that no other device uses. A wrong IP, subnet mask or router value cuts off your Wi-Fi, and you can undo it by setting Configure IP back to Automatic. For a simple IP conflict, try Renew Lease on the same screen, which asks your router to reissue your local address.

Yes. Websites see the VPN server’s IP, not yours. Your ISP can see you’re connected to a VPN server, but the traffic inside is encrypted.

results.title: Building India’s deep-tech enterprise pipeline: from IP to IPO
results.author: mint
results.content:
As entrepreneurial energy plays an ever-larger role in India’s success story, we present a package of weekly opinion articles by members of TiE, a global organization for startups and entrepreneurs. From the rural reach of India’s startup revolution and the easing of capital and compliance challenges to the role of angel investors, how startups and micro, small, and medium enterprises must grow together and how best to track innovation, TiE authors cover a wide spectrum of relevant issues.
***
India’s startup ecosystem is entering a more challenging phase. The focus is shifting from counting startups, patents or funding rounds to evaluating how many Indian technologies move from lab validation to global markets and become established, publicly accountable enterprises.
Beyond the startup count
India has demonstrated significant progress in fostering startups. As of March, the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) had recognized as many as 223,000 startups. Over 13,000 new patent applications were filed by startups, but many were abandoned and only 2,174 were granted. The moot point is that once filed, is the patent for technology differentiation really followed up to create a product for commercialization? Most of these intellectual properties (IPs) are viewed as a “protection” rather than “assets”. And that’s moot in today’s fast-evolving, technology-led world.
Today, nearly 92% of the market capitalization of the S&P 500 is derived from intangible assets—brands, IP, software and data—up from just 17% in 1975. Global spending on intangible investment has crossed $4.7 trillion a year in advanced economies, overtaking investment in physical infrastructure. This is one of the most significant shifts in modern economic history: the countries that lead are no longer those with the largest industrial base, but those that own the world’s most valuable IP and brands. India’s next chapter will therefore be defined not by “Make in India,” but by the ambition to own the world.
India’s real gap is the gap from research to IP, then to products, companies and global scale. Deeptech startups build on scientific breakthroughs in fields like materials, semiconductors, biotech, space, robotics, energy and quantum computing—domains where the IP is not adjacent to the business; it is the business itself. Therefore, the better measure of success is whether a startup becomes a professionally managed enterprise that outlasts its founders.
Deeptech changes the equation
This dynamic creates a fundamentally different development trajectory. Deeptech companies may require several years to transition from laboratory research to commercial scale and face numerous risks. Scientific concepts may not prove viable, and technologies that succeed in laboratory settings can fail in practical applications. Securing regulatory approvals and certifications often requires several years, and customer adoption of new technologies may be slow. These firms typically require multiple funding rounds before generating substantial revenue, thereby increasing capital risk.
Applying expectations of rapid revenue growth, as seen in software companies, can result in premature down-rounds, underinvestment or the abandonment of strategically significant technologies. The implication is evident: deeptech sectors demand not only patient capital but also enduring institutional support, testing facilities, early customers and constant strategic guidance.
What global firms reveal
The most instructive global examples extend beyond narratives of venture funding. They show that deeptech companies are built through coordinated systems spanning research, infrastructure, customer engagement, manufacturing partnerships, long-term technical roadmaps, building talent and, of course, funding.
IBM aims to deliver a large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2029 and is pursuing interim demonstrations of quantum advantage. The lesson: breakthrough technologies attract investment when progress is shown as clear, measurable technical milestones, not vague promises of future disruption.
Emerging artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure firms are commercializing via distribution partnerships. For example, Fundamental raised funding while securing deployment through Amazon Web Services (AWS) infrastructure and customer channels. For Indian deeptech firms, the central question extends beyond funding. It is critical to understand the need for institutions that can facilitate the achievement of technical, industrial and commercial milestones, and the ways through which they can do so.
The bridge is more than money
Over two decades of India’s startup journey, one lesson is clear: capital is only one component of enterprise creation. Entrepreneurs need mentors versed in science and markets, industry partners to test technology, specialized labs, help with regulatory approvals and standards, and tech-transfer offices that protect IP, forge industrial ties, support spin-outs and negotiate founder-friendly licences—plus early-adopter customers and investors.
India needs to move beyond a narrow focus on patent counts. A patent may be legally valid yet commercially insignificant. For deeptech firms, the most valuable IP often extends beyond the patent itself—to proprietary algorithms, industrial designs, scientific datasets, differentiated know-how and trusted brands. With the rapid technology evolution now underway in the country, these are becoming the defining drivers of enterprise value. At IAN, we go further than backing finished products: we invest in companies that are building IP portfolios where commercialization may come much later. That is not easy. It means evaluating the IP, understanding its potential, being extremely patient, and carrying the risk of returns for far longer than a conventional fund is built to do so. And most importantly, invest time and dedicate focused mental energy.
It is common in these IP-focused startups to see the business fundamentals fail, more often than not. During the due diligence, we sometimes discover that the IP is not assigned to the company, or is not protected at all; that the core technology was developed by consultants, leaving the company without ownership of its own code; or that a name, logo or colour has been chosen so close to a much bigger brand that it could one day wipe the company out. It is critical to get all of these well governed, tracked and monitored. Well-protected IP actually is an asse—it supports international expansion, enables licensing, facilitates technology partnerships and improves confidence in future funding rounds.
This is the bet behind companies such as Nayam, Pandorum and Peptris: the wager is on IP creation and its continuous development. Peptris’s IP, for instance, is focused on compressing the drug-discovery cycle from ten years to four or five—and it is already showing success. If that holds, the economics of the pharmaceutical model will change, reducing both the time and the cost of bringing new drugs to market.
Research must move onto the balance sheet
India’s research spending is rising but remains modest. R&D stood at 0.84% of GDP in 2023-24 and is projected to reach 0.90% in 2025-26, with private industry’s share climbing from 32.2% to 45.2% in three years. The direction is right; the gap is still large. China spends about 2.6% of GDP on R&D, the OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development) average is roughly 2.7%, the US 3.7%, South Korea about 5.1%, and Israel leads at 6.3%.
The task, then, is to build a robust public-private partnership. The Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Scheme is the latest instrument designed to strengthen this partnership by enabling industry and private investors to play a significantly greater role. The startup ecosystem is already leading this shift, investing in companies whose value sits in assets that never appear on a traditional balance sheet: brand equity, proprietary technology, patents, customer trust and differentiated know-how. The task now is to bring those assets onto the balance sheet, where they become strategic and defensible.
The prize is real. IAN’s first cheque into Uniphore enabled it to buy an IP asset out of a lab; today the company is valued at over $2.5 billion, with capital from Nvidia and OpenAI—and IAN still holds shares! IP and brand are the new wealth creators, with the ability to transcend geographies and generations.
Technical minds on both sides of the table
Deeptech problems are complex, and the questions that matter cannot be asked from a spreadsheet. A flat quarter in a software company usually signals a demand problem. In a deeptech company, it may be a certification cycle, a material qualification or a pilot waiting on a customer’s timeline. An investor who cannot distinguish delay that is tactical from delay that is strategic will read the first as the second, potentially destroying good companies in the process.
This is what makes patience practical rather than rhetorical. It is not a willingness to wait indefinitely, but the judgement to know what is worth waiting for, and—when fundamentals begin to drift—to intervene with the right questions instead of a devaluation round. India’s deeptech funds, therefore, face a hiring question as much as a fundraising one. Investment teams built to evaluate consumer businesses are not equipped to underwrite scientific risk.
Rethinking capital architecture
The expansion of India’s Fund of Funds architecture is significant because it acknowledges that deeptech sectors require longer-duration, higher-risk capital. Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0, with a proposed corpus of ₹10,000 crore, specifically targets deeptech, technology-driven manufacturing and early-growth companies.
The ₹1 trillion RDI Scheme goes further. It offers long-tenure, low-cost capital to technologies that have been validated in the laboratory, through loans running 12-15 years and equity participation, and it has begun disbursing. A 12- to 15-year horizon is longer than the life of a typical Indian venture fund. That is the point. Public capital is now structured to absorb the technology risk that private capital has never been able to take.
It does not reduce the need for equity investors. It changes what they underwrite. What remains is commercial and institutional risk: the first customer, certification, manufacturing partners and eventually the discipline of being a public company. That is the risk early investors are equipped to take.
Whose problems, whose technology
Decolonizing the academic startup ecosystem should not entail rejecting global science, foreign capital, or international collaboration. Instead, it needs to involve constructing innovation systems grounded in India’s unique needs, capabilities and aspirations.
India’s most consequential technologies may arise from challenges that global markets have historically underestimated, such as affordable medical devices, low-cost water purification or cost-effective space and satellite applications. India can turn local solutions into global opportunities by building proprietary technologies and scalable models. However, it must ensure that the value generated by its innovations is captured domestically, and not allow others to commercialise the intellectual property it creates. The core question is economic sovereignty: who owns the technology, who controls the firm, and where the jobs and manufacturing stay. And, therefore, the role of domestic funding, public or private, extends beyond the financial investment involved—it is the value of sovereignty.
The IPO as institutional maturity
An initial public offering (IPO) is frequently characterized as an exit event. For deeptech companies, it should be seen as more than that—of unleashing domestic monies for building further or creating liquidity for early shareholders. The IPO is not the inevitable destination for every startup; some will be acquired, merged, licensed or remain privately held. Nevertheless, the potential for public-market scale should inform deeptech enterprises’ foundational strategies.
SEDEMAC Mechatronics is instructive. It began in 2007 in an IIT Bombay laboratory, founded by a professor and his students, and listed in March this year—profitable, supplying engine control systems to Tata Motors, Mahindra, Ashok Leyland and TVS. Nineteen years from lab to listing. The offer raised no new capital for the company; every share sold was an existing shareholder’s. The listing was not a fundraising event. It was the point at which a company built on university research became publicly accountable. The benchmark should shift from securing additional funding rounds to becoming a trusted institution within a strategically significant industry.
The pathways still to clear
It would be remiss to suggest that India is already on the perfect path. Several pathways remain to be cleared before IP-led assets create wealth for the country at scale.
Many of the key approval and certification bodies, such as the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), are based outside India. This can make regulatory approvals more time-consuming and expensive for Indian innovators. India, therefore, must develop globally recognized certification and standards bodies of its own to reduce these barriers and strengthen its ability to commercialize IP-led innovations.
Corporate backing for research remains thin. Funding has begun at the early stage through the RDI scheme and a few venture funds. But beyond the Infosys Prize and the Tata Transformation Prize, India lacks corporate funding and recognition for research on the scale of Samsung’s Ho-Am Prize, the Honda Prize or the L’Oréal awards—some of whose supported scientists have gone on to win Nobel Prizes.
India is also grappling with a missing layer of growth capital. Past the early-stage cheques, India does not yet have enough growth capital for scaling companies. Many therefore raise from overseas investors, which means foreign ownership of part of the enterprise—or, in some cases, a decision to flip out of India altogether.
Further, India’s IPO framework does not allow companies with portfolios of IP, but limited profit history, to list on the traditional profit-based main board with its requisite financial track record. They can use the Innovator Growth Platform (IGP), but it does not yet have merchant bankers that understand such companies, or enough investors in the market who do.
In essence, India’s journey towards building IP-led strategic assets is well underway. However, translating these assets into wealth for the country and achieving genuine economic sovereignty will require sustained effort.
Building the missing bridges
This necessitates a national bridge architecture that connects classrooms to laboratories, laboratories to technology-transfer offices, and technology-transfer offices to capable founders. It must also link founders to industrial partners, industrial pilots to procurement processes, procurement to manufacturing, and manufacturing to export markets. It should establish clear pathways for high-growth companies to access public markets and become globally competitive.
Great companies, like the world’s greatest bridges, often begin with ideas that very few people initially believe in. The task before India is to build the spans that carry its research all the way across—Indian-owned, and global in reach.
Padmaja Ruparel is co-founder of the IAN Group and a board member of TiE Delhi-NCR.
This is the eighth part in the series.

### Key Points
- India has recognized over 223,000 startups, but the focus is moving toward converting laboratory research into commercialized, defensible intellectual property assets.
- Deeptech sectors, including semiconductors, biotech, and quantum computing, require patient capital and long-term institutional support rather than rapid, software-style revenue growth.
- The government has introduced the ₹1 trillion Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Scheme and a ₹10,000 crore Fund of Funds to support long-duration, high-risk technology development.

- Companies like Nayam, Pandorum, and Peptris exemplify the shift toward IP-led value creation, aiming to solve complex problems in drug discovery and advanced manufacturing.

### Why it Matters

By fostering institutions that support long-term research and commercialization, India can build globally significant enterprises that secure its economic future and industrial independence.

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories
Los Angeles County election officials say that the Justice Department's list of 20,000 "likely" noncitizens registered to vote is "unreliable," based on their preliminary analysis. A new report from United Nations scientists says that countries are not doing enough to cut emissions that drive climate change, and the United States plays a significant role in climate pollution. The U.S. was the only major economy that saw an increase last year in planet-warming pollution. The report also found that, among G20 countries, the U.S. is tied with Russia for the highest per capita emissions. While China emits more total greenhouse gases annually than the U.S., China's population is more than four times that of the U.S. The rise in U.S. emissions was fueled by increased electricity demand and Trump administration policies that support burning fossil fuels.
Arrests for low-level crimes, including vagrancy and drug possession, increased in the U.S. from 2024 to 2025, according to a new analysis of federal data from the criminal justice and immigration reforms advocacy group FWD.us. The report also highlighted a 188% increase in immigration violations. This comes as violent crime rates, including homicides, dropped to historic lows. The report examined publicly available FBI and immigration arrest data and does not include details about whether charges were dropped or if people served any time in jail or prison. This data covers the first full year of Trump's second term, during which his administration emphasized a tough-on-crime approach. Zoë Towns, the executive director of FWD.us, told NPR ahead of the report's release that the rising trends signal a "really troubling return to some of the extreme law and order policies that defined the American criminal justice system during the '80s and '90s." results.title: SafePay Has Compromised 600 Critical Infrastructure Victims Worldwide, CISA Warns
results.author: James Coker
results.content:
The SafePay ransomware group has compromised at least 600 critical infrastructure organizations, according to a joint advisory issued by government agencies from the US, Germany and UK.
The authoring agencies, which includes the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), warned that since emerging in August 2024, SafePay’s operations have affected a range of businesses and critical infrastructure in North America, South America, Europe and Australia.
The advisory highlighted SafePay’s extensive range of techniques for initial access and post-compromise activities. It urged security teams to take action to mitigate the specific threat posed by SafePay.
It also observed that the actor has been one of the most active ransomware groups in 2026.
A BlacKite report published in June 2026 found that the group was the third most active ransomware group in the first four months of 2026, with the actor focusing its efforts on Germany.
SafePay was also found to be the most active ransomware group in May 2026 by NCC Group, with 70 claimed attacks during the month.
It is believed that SafePay may be a rebrand of several other well-known groups – LockBit, ALPHV/BlackCat and INC Ransomware.
SafePay is believed to be behind the November 2024 ransomware attack on US business services firm Conduent, which resulted in a substantial amount of personal and healthcare data being exfiltrated. On October 16, 2026, Conduent agreed to pay $80m to settle a class action lawsuit related to the data breach.
Range of Initial Access Techniques
The advisory, published by CISA on October 20, highlighted SafePay’s extensive range of initial access vectors. These include credential exposure, implementing brute force password attacks, exploiting virtual private network (VPN) access and exploiting vulnerabilities in edge device products.
Once inside a network, SafePay attackers attempt to gain administrative privileges on existing or newly created accounts to move laterally and access sensitive systems and data. This approach involves using in-built administrative tools consistent with living off the land (LOTL) techniques, such as PsExec, WinRM and remote management and monitoring (RMM) software.
They also employ remote desktop protocol (RDP) to expand their presence within the compromised network.
SafePay actors typically disable security software to avoid detection, and have also been observed using software packing or virtual machine software protection to conceal their code.
To exfiltrate data from victim networks to attacker-controlled accounts, the threat actors use legitimate file transfer tools, such as FileZilla, OneDrive, 7-Zip, RClone and WinRAR.
Following exfiltration, SafePay actors lock victim files using sophisticated hybrid encryption scheme, which combines a ChaCha20 stream cipher with an RSA public-key cryptosystem.
Attackers Pressure Victims Using Phone Calls
The group deploys a double extortion model. It leaves a ransom note on the victim’s system, typically on the desktop or root directory, advising them that SafePay locked their system and to reach out over a chat portal via a TOR .onion link with a victim ID as the login.
SafePay typically demands a subset of company revenue in cryptocurrency in exchange for decryption software.
A representative of the group will also phone victims to increase pressure to pay the extortion demand.
If the organization refuses to pay, SafePay posts the exfiltrated data to its leak website, which is linked in the original ransom note.
How to Protect Against SafePay Attacks
The advisory set out a range of recommendations for security teams to improve their organization’s resiliency to SafePay’s known tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs). These include:
- Prioritize remediating known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs) and keep all operating systems, software, and firmware up to date
- Implement identity, credential, and access management (ICAM) policies across the organization and require MFA for all accounts
- Maintain offline backups of data and regularly test and maintain backup and restoration processes
- Ensure all backup data is encrypted, immutable and covers the entire organization’s data infrastructure
- Implement a recovery plan to maintain and retain multiple copies of sensitive or proprietary data and servers in a physically separate, segmented and secure location
- Segment networks to prevent the spread of ransomware
- Identify, detect and investigate abnormal activity and potential traversal of the indicated ransomware with a network monitoring tool

A joint international advisory warns that the SafePay ransomware group has compromised over 600 critical infrastructure organizations across multiple continents since emerging in August 2024.

### Key Points
- Government agencies from the US, UK, and Germany identified SafePay as a top-tier threat, noting 70 attacks in May 2026 alone.
- The group likely represents a rebrand of established ransomware actors, including LockBit, ALPHV/BlackCat, and INC Ransomware.
- Attackers utilize "living off the land" techniques, exploiting VPNs and edge device vulnerabilities to gain administrative network access.
- SafePay employs a double extortion model, demanding cryptocurrency payments and pressuring victims via direct phone calls.
- Conduent settled a class-action lawsuit for $80 million in October 2026 following a 2024 data breach attributed to the group.

### Why it Matters
The rapid rise of SafePay highlights a significant escalation in the sophistication and frequency of global ransomware operations targeting critical infrastructure. Organizations must prioritize robust identity management and network segmentation to mitigate the severe financial and data-privacy risks posed by these evolving extortion tactics.
